series: Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.2 · October 2026
title: Feebates: The Full Carbon Price at the Margin, Without the Carbon Bill

slides.title: Feebates: The Full Carbon Price at the Margin, Without the Carbon Bill
slides.subtitle: Decarbonizing coal-heavy power and trade-exposed industry
slides.message: A revenue-neutral feebate runs and builds power plants exactly as a carbon tax would, at no cost to the treasury. Under a single buyer it barely moves tariffs; in a wholesale market it raises prices by much less than a tax. The benchmark decides whether it works.
slides.author: Stephen J. Stretton · writing in a personal capacity

slides.text: The tax's relative-price signal cuts emissions; its charge on remaining emissions is a transfer, and that is what governments exempt or hold down.

slides.title: A feebate keeps the incentive and drops most of the bill

points.lead: Above the benchmark, pay; below it, receive.
points.text: Each producer pays the carbon price on the gap between its emissions per unit of output and the sector average.
With the benchmark at the average, the treasury neither gains nor loses.

points.lead: Every tonne cut is worth the full rate,
points.text: as under a tax. Output-based rebating of a tax is the same instrument.

points.lead: The cost is a weaker signal to use less.
points.text: Feebate-and-regulation packages achieve 50–70% of a tax's emission cuts (IMF).

slides.title: Power plants are run and built exactly as under a tax at the same rate

points.text: the benchmark shifts every plant's cost equally, so coal switches to gas at the same price.
the benchmark cancels between clean and coal capacity.
a 6% to 12% cost of capital moves the clean–coal break-even from $8 to $29/tCO₂.

slides.title: In three coal-heavy grids, a feebate keeps regulated tariffs almost flat
slides.note: Most power in all three is sold through state buyers at regulated tariffs today; South Africa legislated for a wholesale market in 2024.
slides.source: Ember yearly electricity data (2024); IPCC (2006); costs illustrative. Working paper 1.2, Table 2.

slides.title: The benchmark must fall as the grid cleans and must not let a dominant utility pay itself

points.lead: A falling average tightens the feebate by itself:
points.text: coal's net fee rises from $11 to $38/MWh over 25 years at $50.

points.lead: Eskom (86% of supply) faces about $7 of a $50 rate.
points.text: Measure large firms against everyone else's average; dispatch on cost plus the full rate.
three benchmarks raise China's cost per tonne by 18%. Keep new plants out of the benchmark for their first years.

slides.source: Working paper 1.2, Propositions 5–6, Figure 2; Goulder et al. (2022); Eskom; NTPC.

slides.title: In industry a feebate protects exporters, and working systems already use benchmarks

points.text: a tax raises producer prices 21–43%, a feebate 7–14% (Brief 1.1).
charges above a standard per unit of output and credits below it; its 2030 price was cut from C$170 to C$115 in May 2026.
pays allowances at a best-10% benchmark times output; it is being phased out for CBAM sectors from 2026.

points.lead: CBAM credits only a price paid, net of rebates,
points.text: so a feebate earns nothing at the border. Credit its carbon-price equivalent (Briefs 1.4, 6.1).

slides.source: Working paper 1.1; Canada OBPS Regulations; ICAP (2026); European Commission; Regulation (EU) 2025/2083.

slides.title: Feebates in use confirm both the incentive and the benchmark warnings

points.text: charge refunded per unit of energy; mean emission rates fell about 40% by 1998, at a rate a tax could not have reached politically.
a fixed benchmark cost about €285m in 2008, and higher sales made the net emissions effect negative.
a carbon price cut power emissions 20.5–26% a year; a feebate keeps that relative-price signal.
